findings.title: Test does not verify the claimed behavior
findings.rationale: The test name asserts that the scan uses the registry default model when no workspace override is saved, but the only assertion is `expect(res.statusCode).toBe(202)`. A 202 response does not confirm which model was used, nor that extraction actually occurred. If the production code had a bug where the model resolution was broken but the endpoint still returned 202 (e.g., a fallback or error swallowed), this test would pass. The test should at minimum verify the extraction result (e.g., check the response body or query the database for the created extraction record and its model).

findings.title: Test does not verify the described model-resolution fallback
findings.rationale: The test asserts only `res.statusCode === 202`. It never checks which model was used, whether the registry default was applied, or that no error occurred due to a missing workspace override. A broken fallback (e.g., always using a hardcoded model or erroring silently) would still pass this test, giving false confidence that the override path works as intended.

findings.title: Test depends on seed data that may change
findings.rationale: The test selects a repo by hardcoded full name `'acme/payments-api'` from the seed. If the seed is updated (e.g., repo names change or the repo is removed), this test will fail. The test does not create its own repo, making it brittle.

findings.title: No verification that extraction produced any result
findings.rationale: The test only checks the HTTP response code. It does not query the database to confirm that conventions were actually stored, nor does it verify the content of the extraction. A 202 could be returned even if the background job fails silently.

findings.title: Test does not verify the model used for extraction
findings.rationale: The test asserts only `res.statusCode === 202`. It never checks which model was selected (e.g., by inspecting the extraction record in the database or the mock's call log). The PR description states the test should verify that 'the scan should use the registry's current default rather than erroring', but the test would pass even if the model-resolution logic is completely broken (e.g., always uses a hardcoded model, or silently falls back to an incorrect model). This is a test that cannot fail while claiming to guard a specific behavior, meeting the CRITICAL threshold.

findings.title: Test does not verify the model used for extraction
findings.rationale: The test asserts only that the response status is 202, but the mock LLM provider returns the same extraction regardless of which model is invoked. This means the test cannot fail if the registry default model is not used (e.g., if a workspace override is incorrectly applied or the default is ignored). The test's name claims it verifies 'scans using the registry default', but the assertion does not establish that.

findings.title: Test implicitly depends on seed state for workspace model override
findings.rationale: The test seeds the database and then selects a repo by name, assuming the seed creates a workspace with no model override. If the seed function is later changed to include a model override (e.g., for another test), this test would silently pass for the wrong reason or fail unexpectedly. The test should explicitly set up the workspace state it requires.

findings.title: Test does not verify the registry default model was used
findings.rationale: The test name and PR description claim the test covers the scenario where the workspace has no model override and the scan uses the registry default. However, the only assertion is that the endpoint returns 202. This test would pass even if the production code uses a hardcoded model, ignores the registry default, or silently falls back to a different model. findings.title: Test does not verify the model resolution behavior it claims to guard
findings.rationale: The test mocks the LLM provider and only asserts that the HTTP status is 202. It does not verify that the registry default model was used, that no workspace override was applied, or that the extraction was actually stored. A regression in the model resolution logic (e.g., always erroring when no override is set) would still pass this test as long as the endpoint returns 202. To properly guard the described scenario, the test should either avoid mocking the LLM or assert on the response body/database state to confirm the correct model was used.

findings.title: Test does not explicitly assert that the workspace has no model override
findings.rationale: The test relies on the seed state to have no workspace model override for the selected repo, but it does not verify this. If the seed changes in the future to set a default override, this test would no longer test the intended scenario without failing. Adding an explicit check or setup to clear any override would make the test more robust.

findings.title: Test does not cover the per-repo grouping logic
findings.rationale: The test inserts two runs for the same PR and asserts `SUM(cost_usd)` equals 0.03. The PR description says this tests the 'per-repo run cost total' which is `SUM(cost_usd) GROUP BY pr_id` as used in the production route. However, the test never groups by `pr_id` or includes multiple PRs for the same repo. It only verifies that summing two rows for a single PR works. A regression that breaks the `GROUP BY` clause (e.g., returning one row per run instead of one row per PR) would not be caught. The test should insert runs for at least two different PRs in the same repo and assert that the query returns two rows with the correct per-PR sums.

findings.title: Silent skip when Docker is unavailable
findings.rationale: If Docker is not available, `beforeAll` returns early and the test body also returns early with `if (!pg) return;`. The test passes without executing any assertions. This can give false confidence in environments where Docker is missing (e.g., some CI runners). Vitest provides `it.runIf` or conditional `it.skip` to make the skip explicit and visible in the test report.

findings.title: Use integer cents for monetary comparison to avoid floating-point issues
findings.rationale: The test uses `toBeCloseTo(0.03)` with default precision (2 decimal places). While this works for the given values, monetary amounts are better handled as integer cents to avoid floating-point rounding surprises. If the schema stores `costUsd` as a `numeric` or `float`, the sum could have more than 2 decimal places and `toBeCloseTo` with default precision might mask small errors. Using `expect(Number(row.costUsd) * 100).toBe(3)` (or converting to cents in the query) would be more robust.

findings.title: Entire new feature module has no tests
findings.rationale:
The PR introduces a complete share module with 7 endpoints, a service layer, a repository with raw SQL queries, shell command execution (`execSync`), password hashing, template rendering, and a client component — yet **no test files are added or modified**. This means every code path is untested, including:

- SQL injection vectors in `repository.ts` (lines 22, 37, 52, 66) where user-controlled `token` and `sort` values are interpolated directly into SQL strings.
- Shell injection in `service.ts` (lines 72, 97) where `digestId` and `label` are interpolated into `execSync` commands.
- Error handling in the client component (`SharedDigestView.tsx` line 14) where a failed fetch only sets an error message string with no logging or fallback.
- Authorization bypass: the public share endpoints intentionally skip workspace context, but there is no test verifying that a token cannot be used to access another workspace's data.
- Password gate logic: `hashSharePassword` uses MD5 (a weak hash), and there is no test confirming that password-protected shares actually require the password before rendering.

Because the entire feature is untested, any of these issues would go undetected by the test suite. This is a CRITICAL finding that blocks merge.

findings.title: No tests for code injection via `new Function` in renderTemplate
findings.rationale: `renderTemplate` uses `new Function(...keys, `return (${expr});`)` to evaluate arbitrary expressions from the digest body. If an attacker can control the digest body (e.g., by creating a digest with malicious markdown), they can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server. There are zero tests for this function. A test that passes a body containing `{{ process.env.SECRET }}` would immediately reveal the vulnerability.

findings.title: No tests for client-side XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML
findings.rationale: The `SharedDigestView` component renders server-provided HTML via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. If the server does not sanitize the digest HTML (e.g., if `renderTemplate` or the markdown renderer allows `<script>` tags), this is a stored XSS vector. There are zero tests for this component. A test that mocks the API to return HTML containing `<script>alert(1)</script>` would verify whether the component or server sanitizes it.

findings.title: No tests for hardcoded secrets in constants.ts
